meta_description: Apartment complex insurance appraisal explained: how it works, why multi-family claims get disputed, and how Texas owners recover.
h1: Apartment Complex Insurance Appraisal: A Guide for Texas Owners
excerpt: How does apartment complex insurance appraisal work? Learn when to invoke it, why multi-family claims are hard to settle and how Texas owners can document damage across every building.
key_takeaways: Appraisal resolves amount-of-loss disputes when coverage on an apartment claim is accepted.
Small pricing or quantity errors multiply across many buildings.
Document damage building by building and unit by unit, including tenant reports.
Loss of rents disputes often accompany property damage disputes.
Choose an appraiser experienced with large multi-building losses.
body_html:
An apartment complex insurance appraisal is a process in the property policy for resolving disputes over the amount of loss on a multi-family claim. When the owner and insurer agree damage is covered but disagree on the cost, each side names an appraiser, and an umpire settles any remaining differences. It is often faster and less costly than litigation.

What is an apartment complex insurance appraisal?

Most commercial property policies that cover apartment communities contain an appraisal clause. It gives either party the right to demand appraisal when they cannot agree on the amount of loss. The process works the same way it does on a home, but the scale is very different.

Here is how it typically works:

  1. One party sends a written demand for appraisal under the policy.
  2. Each side selects a competent, disinterested appraiser, usually within a deadline set by the policy.
  3. The two appraisers select an umpire. If they cannot agree, a court can generally appoint one.
  4. The appraisers inspect the property, exchange estimates and try to agree on the amount of loss.
  5. Items they cannot agree on go to the umpire.
  6. An award signed by any two of the three sets the amount of loss.

In Texas, appraisers decide the amount of loss and may assess damage and causation questions tied to that amount, but they do not decide coverage. That framework comes from State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009). This is general information, not legal advice.

When does an apartment complex insurance appraisal make sense?

Appraisal fits when coverage is accepted but the numbers are not. Common triggers include:

  • A carrier estimate far below the owner's contractor or consultant estimate
  • Disputes over repairing versus replacing roofs, siding or windows
  • Buildings, units or components left out of the scope
  • Disagreement over code upgrade costs
  • Stalled or unpaid supplemental claims
  • Partial payments with no clear path to resolution

Appraisal also helps when negotiations have simply stalled. On large multi-family losses, claims can drag on for months while adjusters, engineers and consultants trade reports. A formal appraisal demand moves the dispute into a defined process with a decision at the end.

Before invoking, owners should weigh the amount in dispute against the cost of appraisal and consider whether the disagreement is really about coverage, which appraisal does not decide.

Why apartment complex claims are so complicated

An apartment community is not one building. It is a collection of structures and systems, each with its own damage, materials and repair needs:

  • Multiple residential buildings, often of different ages or designs
  • Clubhouses and leasing offices
  • Pools, fitness centers and amenity buildings
  • Carports and detached garages
  • Maintenance facilities
  • Fencing, gates and site lighting

Many types of damage at once

ComponentTypical storm damageEstimating challenge
RoofingHail bruising, granule loss, wind-lifted shinglesDozens of roofs, each measured separately
HVAC unitsFin damage, condenser impactsLarge unit counts; repair vs replacement
Gutters and downspoutsDents and deformationLinear footage across many buildings
Siding and trimCracks, punctures, chipped paintMatching across entire elevations

On a large complex, a small error in unit price or quantity is multiplied across every building. A missed line item worth a few hundred dollars per building can become a significant amount across the property.

Occupied units add friction

Interior damage is harder to document when tenants live in the units. Owners face scheduling conflicts, limited inspection windows, tenants who report leaks late or not at all, and incomplete records. Some interior damage may not be discovered until weeks after the storm. Turnover adds another wrinkle, since damage in a vacant unit may be repaired during make-ready before anyone photographs it.

Tip: Send a written notice to all residents after a storm asking them to report leaks, stains and broken windows. A dated log of tenant reports is strong evidence of when interior damage occurred.

Common insurance claims at apartment complexes

Hail damage

Hail is the most common source of apartment claims in Texas. It affects shingles and metal roofs, HVAC units, skylights, gutters, screens, siding and paint. The biggest disputes are usually whether roofs need full replacement and whether damage is cosmetic or functional.

Wind damage

High winds lift and remove shingles, tear off siding and soffit, damage fencing and carports, and drive rain into building envelopes.

Water damage

Storm-created openings, burst pipes during freezes and failed plumbing can damage multiple units at once, especially in stacked buildings where water travels between floors.

Fire damage

Apartment fires often damage adjacent units through smoke, heat and water from firefighting, which leads to disputes over the extent of affected areas.

For more on recurring issues, see multi-family insurance claim disputes.

How to document apartment complex damage

Strong documentation wins appraisals. For a multi-family property, organize evidence building by building and unit by unit.

  1. Map the property: number every building and list its roof type, siding, windows and HVAC units.
  2. Photograph each building on all elevations and every roof slope, with test squares where hail is involved.
  3. Log interior damage by unit with dates, tenant reports and photos.
  4. Capture 3D scans of damaged interiors and common areas before repairs.
  5. Keep maintenance and roof records to rebut age and wear arguments.
  6. Collect weather data for the date of loss.
  7. Track mitigation costs for tarping, water extraction and emergency repairs.

Our Matterport 3D documentation service is especially useful on multi-family losses, because a full record of every affected unit and common area can be shared with adjusters, appraisers and umpires without repeated site visits.

Loss of rents and business income

When units become uninhabitable, owners lose rental income. Many apartment policies include loss of rents or business income coverage to replace that income during the restoration period. Disputes often arise over how long restoration should reasonably take and how much rent was actually lost.

Whether the appraisal clause applies to business income depends on the policy language and the nature of the dispute. Read business interruption vs property damage claims to understand how these coverages differ.

Apartment complex insurance appraisal in Texas

Texas has one of the largest multi-family markets in the country, concentrated in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin and San Antonio. Many of those communities sit squarely in hail country, and Gulf Coast properties face hurricane wind and water. Freeze events can also burst pipes across entire complexes.

Key Texas rules owners should know:

  • Prompt payment: under Tex. Ins. Code ch. 542, insurers generally must acknowledge a claim within 15 days and accept or reject it within 15 business days after receiving requested information.
  • Pre-suit notice: for weather-related claims, Chapter 542A generally requires written notice at least 61 days before filing suit.
  • Appraisal and later claims: the Texas Supreme Court's 2019 decisions in Barbara Technologies and Ortiz address how payment of an appraisal award affects prompt payment and other extra-contractual claims.

Commercial policies also often carry per-building or per-occurrence deductibles, sometimes as a percentage of insured value. How the deductible applies across many buildings can change the net recovery significantly.

Common mistakes in apartment complex insurance appraisal

Owners who handle multi-family appraisal well tend to avoid the same set of errors. The most common mistakes we see are:

  • Invoking appraisal too early, before the full scope is known and before supplements have been submitted.
  • Using a single lump-sum estimate instead of a building-by-building breakdown the panel can verify.
  • Ignoring the umpire selection. The umpire decides contested items, so experience with commercial and multi-family losses matters.
  • Letting repairs erase the evidence, such as replacing roofs or remodeling units before damage is documented.
  • Overlooking policy deadlines for naming an appraiser or responding to the other side's demand.
  • Treating coverage disputes as pricing disputes, which appraisal cannot fix.

Learn how umpires fit into the process on our insurance umpire services page. A well-chosen, impartial umpire who understands multi-family construction helps the panel reach a sound award on the items the appraisers cannot resolve.

Timing matters too. An apartment complex insurance appraisal works best once the owner has a complete, documented scope and the carrier has had a fair chance to respond to supplements. Going in prepared shortens the process and keeps the panel focused on real differences.

Choosing an appraiser for an apartment claim

The appraiser you select should be independent and experienced with large, multi-building losses. Look for someone who can:

  • Inspect and document dozens of buildings efficiently
  • Write detailed Xactimate or Symbility estimates by building
  • Understand commercial roofing, siding and HVAC systems
  • Present evidence clearly to the other appraiser and the umpire
  • Handle matching, code and repair-versus-replace arguments

Learn more in our guides to commercial property insurance appraisal in Texas and large loss insurance appraisal in Texas. If you manage a condominium or townhome community, the HOA insurance appraisal process is similar.

Next steps for apartment owners and managers

Start with documentation: a building-by-building record of damage, tenant reports and maintenance history. Compare the carrier's estimate against a detailed independent estimate for each structure. If the gap remains after supplements and negotiation, an apartment complex insurance appraisal can bring the dispute to a decision without the cost and delay of a lawsuit.

faqs.q: How long does an apartment complex insurance appraisal take?
faqs.a: Timelines vary with the size of the property, the number of buildings and how far apart the estimates are. Smaller disputes may resolve in a few months, while large multi-building losses can take longer, especially if an umpire must decide many items. Organized documentation and responsive appraisers shorten the process.

faqs.q: Who pays for an apartment insurance appraisal?
faqs.a: Under most appraisal clauses, each party pays its own appraiser and the two sides split the umpire's fees equally. Policy wording controls, so check your appraisal clause. Owners should compare the expected cost with the amount in dispute before invoking appraisal on a multi-family claim.

faqs.q: Can appraisal include every building at the complex?
faqs.a: Appraisal generally covers the disputed amount of loss for the claim, which can include all damaged buildings and components under that claim. The appraisal demand and the scope of the dispute define what the panel addresses. Coverage questions, such as whether a building was damaged by a covered peril at all, may be handled separately.

faqs.q: Does appraisal cover loss of rents?
faqs.a: It depends on the policy language and the type of disagreement. Some policies apply the appraisal clause to all amounts of loss, including business income or rental value, while others are less clear. Owners should review the policy and get advice before assuming loss of rents will be part of the appraisal.

faqs.q: Do tenants have a role in apartment claim appraisal?
faqs.a: Tenants are not parties to the owner's property insurance appraisal, but their cooperation matters. Access to units for inspections, timely reports of leaks and photos of interior damage all strengthen the owner's documentation. Tenants' own belongings are typically covered under their renters insurance, not the owner's policy.
